news.title: Can you safely use a 140w charger on an iPhone?
news.summary: Yalcin Sonat/Shutterstock Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover The simple answer is yes, an iPhone can tolerate a 140-watt charger, but it's not a simple process, and there are safety considerations. A 140-watt charger is an upper limit that your iPhone will never reach because even the latest iPhone 18 Pro hits its cap at 52W. An iPhone can only pull what it can pull, and it's nowhere near 140W. USB PD used to top out at 100W, but the newer range is between 100W and 240W, now known as Extended Power Range (EPR). EPR adds 28V, 36V and 48V options. Once a device is in EPR mode, it has to send a "keep-alive" message every half second.

news.title: USC engineers built a smart ring that monitors stress by taking a peek at your sweat glands
news.summary: Stress tracking on wearables like the Fitbit Sense usually relies on electrodermal activity, or EDA. The method measures changes in skin conductance caused by sweat glands, but it needs electrodes to stay in steady contact with your skin. But there are a few drawbacks to this approach. You need to place your hand over the wearable to enable skin contact, and keep it that way for a couple of minutes. That also means every time you want to check stress levels, you need to take a break and perform the sensing exercise because it doesn't perform continuous stress monitoring. We may finally have an entirely new approach to stress-sensing that uses light-based analysis for a more accurate analysis, and something with a framework so frugal that the whole chore can run entirely on the ring itself.

news.title: Your phone habits could be reflected in your brain, new study suggests
news.summary: Spending hours glued to a phone or tablet might leave more than a dent in productivity. A new study from researchers at the University of Eastern Finland has found associations between screen time and differences in the brain structure of teenagers. MRI scans revealed changes in grey matter volume across regions involved in memory, attention, decision-making, and visual processing. Before anyone declares smartphones the villain, though, there's an important caveat: the study found associations, not proof that screens directly cause these changes. Published in NeuroImage: Reports, the study examined 44 healthy adolescents aged 16 to 19, including 25 girls and 19 boys. Researchers used MRI scans to measure grey matter volume and questionnaires to assess leisure screen time, smart device use, and physical activity.

news.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
news.summary: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended.

news.summary: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language.
